#8218. How To Make Summer Memories That Stick

Summer’s behind us. What memories did you make?

Labor day is upon us and as I celebrate the ending of the chaotic mess that is summer for parents, I also can’t help but feel a little wistful. Did I make the most of the summer? Or, more to the point, have I made lasting memories for my kids?

The answer to that, I think, is yes. But the memories are not found in volumes of ice cream, the rides at the county fair, the hours of pool time and picnics, or the (shockingly expensive) songs and bonding they had at camps. I believe that in the long term these simple joys will become part of a happy and balanced childhood, but they’re not the kind of thing they look back on and say, “remember when …?”

The “remember when” moments are a different kind of fun — Type 2 fun.

As former Fatherly editor Julia Holmes explained in her wonderful essay on memory and adventures, there are varying levels of fun. “The ‘fun scale,’” she writes, “which first circulated in climbing books and media in the 1980s, divides outdoor recreation into three major categories. At one end of the scale is Type 1: You expect to enjoy yourself and you do (a day at the beach). At the other end of the scale is Type 3: not even remotely fun, catastrophically bad, something never to be repeated (shipwrecked). Somewhere between those extremes is the perfect fun, the kind of fun that pushes you past yourself and (hopefully) delivers you back to yourself in better condition — stronger, happier, full of fresh gratitude for comfort and company.”

Type 2 fun is the stuff of memories. When we tell a great story about travel or adventure — one that’s worth retelling throughout life — there is usually an edge to it. There are barriers overcome, there is a sketchy or frightening moment, there are lessons learned.

I think about Type 2 fun all the time. As a distance runner and cyclist and outdoors person who remembers the first time they got hypothermia fondly (it’s a good story!), I embrace such “fun” and try to bring my kids into it. As a dad, I know that summers, with the kids out of school and the weather cooperating is a great time to go after it.

So, as we stare down Labor Day, I wonder to myself, how’d I do?

This summer, if you are to look at my 8-year-old’s skinned knees, I think some memories were made. We daily took to the trails and roads and pump track to bike. There were falls, tears, and an awesome amount of getting back on the bike with a chin held high. One of his favorite stories to tell was actually from last summer when we were mountain biking together, attached, tandem-style. It was hot, buggy, and we had already had a minor crash (or two) along the rocky trail. At one point, there was a ledge that required you to walk your bike, single file, over a small cliff. I asked my son to go to the other side and wait, the better for him to watch as I awkwardly pushed the long tandem bike along the thin ledge, lost my balance and, rather than fall 20 feet to the forest floor, tossed the bike and leaned into the rock. I steadied myself as the bike crashed below. Thirty minutes later, we had were back up top and on the trail again — with a story to tell.

For my older child, I might have gone a little hard on the Type 2 fun this summer. I offered to pick up my teen and their best friend from overnight camp and take them on their first real backpacking trip this year. I marked the maps, packed the food, and neatly stored our tents, stoves, water purifiers, headlamps, and sleeping bags for a three-night, four day trip on The Long Trail in Vermont. The more serious ascent was to happen on day 1, leaving the rest of the trip for a rolling hike, out and back, to give them a pleasant taste for one of my favorite pastimes.

The Gods of Type 2 fun had other plans. First of all, the parking lot on the map simply wasn’t where it should have been, so we wound our way through country roads to the next lot, miles away and downhill from the planned start. In the new parking lot, a sign informed us that a shelter had moved a few miles further. The short of it: A good hike became a formidable trek. Three days, 18.34 miles, and 4,698 feet (up!) later, the kids refused to camp a third night in the woods, demanding to hike straight to the car and go get a hotel. We did just that. I stopped for milkshakes on the way, but somehow, years from now, I don’t think the truck stop shakes are what they’re going to remember about their time on The Long Trail.

This weekend, I think I’m going to take the family to Coney Island. The kids will grab hot dogs, we’ll all ride on the Wonder Wheel, walk down the beach and share the breeze. We’ve made enough memories this summer — and everyone needs a little forgettable fun too.

#8215. How To Get Fantastic Sleep

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

On a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a big fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

For the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and issues that are familiar to all kids. One big one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

Now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a new Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

So what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

It’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

When my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find new fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

#8213. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Tired of the practically impossible task of packing up the family for a holiday? Here are the best packing cubes for busy families on the go.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

Unleash your little one's love for Lightning McQueen with these top-rated Cars playsets and figures.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:

Of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!)

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or shows, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

The stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Traveling with kids doesn't;t have to mean getting rid of your entire beauty routine.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

My family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

The fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Could your child use a little encouragement to read? Disney is here to help with these fabulous books for kids ages 5 to 9.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

#8212. 10 Questions Worth Asking At Your Annual Physical After Age 40, According To Doctors

They want to talk to you about prevention, prevention, and more prevention.

Between work, kids, kids’ extracurriculars, family obligations, and everything else, it’s easy, as moms, to let our own health fall by the wayside. If nothing’s bothering you, of course your annual physical is the first thing to get canceled in a week loaded with other appointments and to-dos. But doctors agree that while moms are often the last people to complain about feeling tired, rundown, or off, they also tend to wait too long to bring their concerns to a medical provider, as Scary Mommy previously reported. So, this is your sign to keep that annual physical and use it to talk to your doctor about all the health concerns that come with aging. While you might be fine now, your doctor is eager to tell you how to keep it that way.

“Cardiovascular disease is the number one killer in the United States for both men and women. In order to live a long and happy life you need to understand your risk for developing cardiovascular disease and how to combat and lower your risk,” says Dr. Colleen Reidy, DO, is a family medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

“This is the blood work that I recommend for most patients,” says Reidy. “CMP will evaluate electrolytes, kidney function, and liver function. A CBC will look into your blood counts. Ferritin level will screen for iron deficiency, which can be the first sign of colon cancer. Lipoprotein a and LDL/lipid panel can give us insight into your risk for high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease. If you are obese or have a family history of diabetes, you might want to consider getting your A1C checked to rule out pre-diabetes or diabetes.”

Make sure you discuss any family history of cancer with your primary care provider while you’re at it. “Age-based cancer screening allows for early detection of certain types of cancers and reduces cancer mortality,” says Dr. Jacqueline Jepsen, family medicine physician at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

Your family history may influence when screening should begin and how frequently it should be performed, according to Dr. Harold Jaimes, board-certified internal medicine physician and owner of Jaimes Medical Group in Chicago.

“Always tell your doctor about any family history of cancer, especially when relatives were diagnosed at a younger age. This can significantly change screening recommendations,” he says.

“Routine colon cancer screening now begins at age 45 for most people, rather than 50. Be sure to tell your doctor if anyone in your family has had colon cancer, particularly at a younger age,” Jaimes says.

You might be at higher risk of colon cancer — and therefore require screening at an earlier age — if you have a history of radiation to the abdomen, inflammatory bowel disease, or certain types of polyps, according to the American Cancer Society.

“Age 40 is the year to start doing routine yearly mammograms. If you have dense breast tissue, then you might qualify for follow-up ultrasound,” Reidy says.

Women should stay current with cervical cancer screening, including Pap smears and/or HPV testing, as appropriate for their age and medical history, Jaimes adds. New guidelines allow for women to self-swab the vagina at home to be screened for HPV. If you’re someone who struggles with annual well woman visits, talk to your OB-GYN about this option.

Keeping up with the recommended vaccine schedule is an important part of disease prevention that boosts personal immunity and herd immunity, Jepsen says.

“The average age of menopause in America is 51 years old. However, the perimenopausal phase can last a few years and can look different in everyone. It’s good to talk to your doctor about what to look out for,” says Reidy.

Women, especially after menopause, are at risk of decreased bone density, Reidy points out. As Scary Mommy previously reported, you can maintain bone density with exercise, like strength training two to three times per week or adding walks, and even dancing, into your day-today. Bringing up osteoporosis with your doctor allows them to talk to you about any potential risk factors too.

“You might want to talk to your doctor about any chronic conditions, like celiac disease, or long-term use of steroids that might put you at increased risk of osteoporosis and warrant earlier screening,” Reidy says.

Exercising isn’t just about your weight; it turns out that your muscle mass is the best indicator of your longevity and quality of life as you age.

Most doctors recommend 150 minutes of moderate intensity exercise per week, but it’s important to talk to your doctor about what that means for you, Reidy says. Make a plan with your provider that takes into account your unique medical history, risk factors, and lifestyle.

“As we age, certain hormone levels change, and this is normal,” Jepsen says. “It is important to discuss with your doctor what signs of aging you should expect and what symptoms are ‘red flag’ symptoms, meaning you should reach out to your doctor to discuss further.”

“I remind my patients that many serious medical conditions develop silently, long before symptoms appear. Annual visits give us an opportunity to identify problems early, address risk factors, and hopefully prevent more serious illness down the road,” says Jaimes. “After all, we wouldn’t think twice about maintaining our cars to keep them running for years. Shouldn’t we give our own bodies at least the same attention?”

#8210. The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have said,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The New York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”

Bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

We’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a big piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

#8209. The 14 Best Winter Comfort Foods That Aren't Soup

Warm, satisfying, delicious dishes you can chew.

I’m going to be vulnerable with you here: I don’t like soup that much. I know! I know. Burn me at the stake. Soup can be delightful and certainly has its place, but for me, soup will never satisfy in the same way as, I dunno, any other warm and savory food you can chew. If you’re with me, then you also probably look forward to your favorite winter comfort foods that aren’t soup. From pastas with savory sauces to giant pots of piping hot chili, these are some of my favorites to fall back on all throughout the coldest season of the year.

It’s hot, cheesy, carby, and filling — yep, Damn Delicious’ creamy beef and shells is a bona fide comfort dish. It’s essentially a homemade version of Hamburger Helper, and it’s one your family will ask for again and again.

Chili is the ultimate comfort meal, in my opinion. All The Healthy Things’ recipe is super easy — just brown your meat, dice your veg, and dump everything into the slow cooker for five to six hours on high or seven to eight on low. The best part of chili is adding all your favorite toppings, so don’t forget the avocados, cheese, and crushed Fritos.

Laughing Spatula’s cheesy chicken and broccoli casserole is so good when you’re feeding a crowd, and it’s particularly easy to make if you have some leftover chicken breasts lying around that you need to use up. Serve it with some garlic bread for maximum comfort.

Shepherd’s pie is one of those dishes I love but always seem to forget about when I’m planning what to make for dinner. Princess Pinky Girl’s version is super simple and uses instant mashed potatoes to speed things up, and overall is a surprisingly affordable meal for how many servings it yields.

When I think about the effort that goes into making a homemade soup, I think... what if I put the same amount of effort into something made of pasta instead? Averie Cooks’ homemade lasagna is such a great comfort meal for wintertime. It’s hot, saucy, cheesy, and just everything you could want.

If you were also introduced to beef bourguignon in the movie Julie & Julia, you were probably intimidated out of ever trying to cook it for yourself. Laughing Spatula’s version is much simpler because it’s made in the slow cooker and doesn’t require so much time and attention. You still get all the savory, herby deliciousness, which is what matters.

Dude That Cooks’ yellow fish curry feels nostalgic for me; when it was wintertime in college, I’d hit up the local Indian restaurant for yellow curry quite a bit. If a solid, spicy curry is what warms your bones best, you’ll be very happy with all the authentic flavor of this recipe.

Something about eating like I’m at a medieval tavern comforts my soul — the thought of crusty bread, a hunk of cheese, and a roast chicken feels like a balm against the winter cold. All The Healthy Things’ recipe will help you make a flavorful bird that’s done all the way through (and you should definitely eat those carrots in celery when they’re done — yum).

Chicken and dumplings is the comfort food in the South, and if you’ve never tried it, I urge you to make Princess Pinky Girl’s version. It’s a delicious, creamy chicken base with floating, fluffy dumplings bobbing throughout, and it’s ready in 30 minutes. Ugh, it’s just so good when you’ve been out in the cold all day.

Mac and cheese but make it seasonal? Twist my arm... Feel Good Foodie’s recipe for pumpkin mac and cheese is incredibly simple and requires very few ingredients. You could definitely toss in some chicken and broccoli to make this a more filling meal-in-a-bowl too.

Fried rice topped with a runny egg is a top tier comfort food. Damn Delicious’ version, kimchi fried rice, is even more delicious than your average bowl and you know the spice will help clear your sinuses and warm you up too.

I love an Averie Cooks’ recipe when I want to get maximum flavor out of minimal time spent in the kitchen. Her slow cooker Tuscan chicken offers just that, with a creamy, comforting Parmesan and sun-dried tomato sauce that’ll have you coming back to the Crockpot for seconds.

When nothing else sounds good, enchiladas always do. They’re hot and melty and cheesy and saucy and just...comforting. Simply LaKita’s are more exciting than your usual chicken or ground beef enchiladas. Hers are stuffed with chorizo, sweet potatoes, and a little bit of spinach, so you’re still getting your veggie servings in, don’t worry.

Welp, time to go drag my slow cooker back out again.

#8206. What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he said to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”

Finally, he says that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

#8204. The Promise & Peril Of Mom Friends

You may love them or hate them, but, for a huge chunk of time, you need them.

When my kids were younger, I had a few groups of women I considered my “mom friends” — the mothers of my children’s friends. Even if you don’t have mom friends, you’re probably aware of mom groups; the media loves them, the more gossipy and scandalous, the better. You’ll see it in the first-hand reports of toxic celebrity-mom group chats and mega-hits like Big Little Lies, which features rich moms, working-class moms, and a murder. These friendships are a focal point of our cultural imagination, where society can project all our ideas and expectations of women raising children in these times. But far from the media and the memes, mom groups are complicated. A source of comfort and camaraderie, yes, but also awkwardness — and sometimes even distress.

The good stuff first: there’s a lot to love about friendships with other mothers. They’re a built-in support network, there when you need them. There is always someone available to pick up your kid when you’re stuck in traffic or give a cuddle when they’re scared at a sleep over. They have an extra pair of shin pads at the soccer tournament when you forgot to pack them, or a nut-free snack on the field trip for your highly-allergic toddler. Underneath the relief these encounters engender lies a deeper and implicit exchange of trust. It says: Please take care of my kid. Please make sure they are cared for, supported, seen, loved. When we’re at our best, we’re working towards a shared goal: helping to raise each other’s children. Building and sustaining the village. There’s joy in that; a bit of magic, too.

These friendships also provide a rare space where we can acknowledge the realities of motherhood, the impossible things asked of women raising children. Whatever it is that’s weighing you down — a partner who calls caring for his own children “babysitting,” unhelpful administrators for a kid struggling at school, a job that won’t give you paid leave — other mothers have undoubtedly been there. They can confirm for you the ways in which society pretends to revere mothers in theory but crushes them in practice, and can help you find laughter in the absurdity of it all.

And yet. These friendships, so tender and interdependent in some ways, can also be a source of unease. It is sometimes tricky to figure out just how much of ourselves to share, and how much we really want to know about the other women in our proverbial village. Some of what we find out inadvertently is funny, or endearing, or the kind of information that brings us closer. On the school group chat we’ll find another mom who has the same sarcastic sense of humor, or who also hates the same teacher that we do. We find out which mom is a Scientologist, which one brags incessantly about her kids. Occasionally we’ll find out intimate things when someone seeks advice about a breast lump or impending separation that she hasn’t told the kids about yet.

But there are other times when scratching below the surface of these friendships and seeing what’s underneath is more complicated. For me, that often involves learning things about other mothers that I wish I hadn’t known. Because knowing requires a decision: what then? What do I do? Or say? Or not say? And, on the flip side, how much do I want to reveal about myself and my own opinions?

My kids go to an international school with a very diverse group of families from all over the world, with wildly different priorities and values than my own. I’m not just talking about voting differently (though there’s that, too); there are moms at school who are anti-immigrant or make jokes about gay people or have blinding amounts of wealth. Some of them yell at their nannies in front of me. Some don’t make their kids wear seatbelts. They think and talk and parent differently than I do. And I’m sure some of them don’t like or agree with me, find me self-righteous or judgmental, with no sense of humor. (Fair on 1 and 2, wrong on 3!) I’m sure I’m not everyone’s cup of tea, either.

For years in situations like these, I struggled to figure out where to draw the line, if at all; if my kids were physically safe, was there anything else I truly needed to consider before I agreed to that playdate or sleepover? Were there questions to ask? And if I didn’t like what I learned, what was I supposed to do rearrange carpool? Encourage my kids to find other friends, so that I didn’t have to socialize and rely on people I didn’t agree with? Is that possible? Perhaps more importantly, is it worth it?

When one of my kids was little and starting a new school, I met a mom at back-to-school night. I mentioned my work with human rights for migrant workers; she went on what I can only describe as a diatribe, without irony, about how domestic workers (the poorest and least protected of the working poor) are entitled and demanding and need to be paid less. And then she promptly invited my kid to a birthday party. Should I have declined the invitation? Said no and argued all night about international labor standards? Said yes and argued about labor standards? Did I even want to engage? In that case, it turned out, I did not. I wanted to go to a birthday party and eat cupcakes and exchange Lego gifts and not have to always be my full self, not have to ponder whether to respond when someone makes an off-color comment, risking either conflict or complicity. I wanted to make small talk, to think about what we have in common (our kids and their friendship), not what separates us (everything else).

Now that my kids are older, the complications of mom friendships have lost some of their intensity. In part, it’s because I don’t rely on other mothers as much as I used to; the days of chaperones and carpools have passed. And my kids have grown, have developed their own opinions and worldviews, largely unaffected by their friends’ parents, despite my fears. Like most teenagers, they’re discerning; they’ve identified a few adults they admire and have written off the rest. And I’ve seen that one of the benefits of living in a community with people who are so different from us is that my family has had more explicit conversations about topics like wealth and race and privilege than we might have had in a social world where people’s behaviors and choices looked like ours.

I realized, too, that my judgements of other moms for the ways they vote or talk or act, or my concerns about their judgements of me — they didn’t matter that much. After all, we weren’t close enough to really change each other’s minds about anything of substance. We weren’t real friends, we were mom friends. I can recognize this category of relationships for what they were: intimate and interdependent, and somehow still distant. I can acknowledge that these mom friends lived and talked in ways that were troubling to me, and that I also appreciated the role they played in my kids’ lives. And I’m reminded, of course, that this is what having a proverbial village is all about; back when our foremothers raised kids in actual villages, they weren’t all best friends, they probably didn’t even like each other that much.

They just had to know that they were there.

Saba Brelvi is a Muslim American writer from California. She holds a BA from Brown University and an MPH from Johns Hopkins University and has spent more than two decades working in the nonprofit sector. She currently resides in Abu Dhabi with her family. The Squatters is her debut novel.

#8202. Are Our Chidlren Really So Mentally Unwell?

American kids are having a mental health crisis like no other. What are we to do with all these diagnoses?

In a New York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another. Many exist in a gray zone that previous generations of parents never encountered.”

For those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious. For those with younger ones, buckle up.

In Yang’s story, she focuses on the role schools play. Failures in education may lead to an increase of psychiatric diagnoses like ADHD — alongside IEPs or maybe medications — as a means to catch up kids who are being lost in crowded, test-reliant, merit-funded schools. Of course, even Yang points out that schools are only one part of the puzzle. There’s screens and social media taking over our emotional lives and psychiatric development; the pandemic’s long-felt chilling effect on socialization; the adult world of division and anger in politics and everywhere else; and of course changes within the Mental Health Industrial Complex.

It’s this last piece that Dr. Sami Timimi, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychotherapist at the National Health Service in the United Kingdom is focused on. He's the author of six books including Naughty Boys: Anti-Social Behavior, ADHD, and the Role of Culture and his most recent book, Searching for Normal, which promises to outline a new approach to understanding mental health, distress and neurodiversity. There little doubt we could use some advice here — and a bit of demystification around the mental health crises that seems to have taken over childhood.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I frankly found Searching for Normal to be a difficult book. The science and ideas are very clearly laid out, but you're throwing a lot of stones systemically and culturally that are not often cast. As a layperson and a parent with a house filled with diagnoses, medications, cultural shame, and lots of doubts about our mental health journey, the paralysis you describe feels very close to home. Given all this, I'm wondering, big picture, what is the main takeaway you'd want a parent to walk away with from your book?

Dr. Sami Timimi: It is a difficult read because we have a public narrative that's been around for a while that's really created a mythology around what we think of in terms of mental health and behavioral difference. My main message is that what we are calling psychiatric diagnosis aren't really diagnoses. And be careful where the culture of diagnoses might lead you to, because we have so much evidence now that the way we're approaching mental health has resulted in something called the treatment prevention paradox, where at a population level we're seeing increasing prevalence of mental conditions and mental health diagnoses. At the same time we're seeing an increasing number of people accessing various types of treatments associated with these diagnoses.

But we're not seeing an improvement in the outcomes. If we saw an improvement in the outcomes, we would expect at least a stabilization and hopefully a reduction in prevalence of certain conditions because they would be being effectively treated. I don't think there's actually much disagreement with this in most of the academic literature on what's going on because mental health does seem to be an outlier compared to we've seen a lot of progress in physical health.

For example, when I was a kid, if I got leukemia, my chances of survival into adulthood was around 20%. Now it's around 80%. So this is what happens when you have approaches that are built on technical knowledge that allows you to understand what's going on and make specific treatments for it. But it seems to be the case in mental health that we're going in the wrong direction. What are the assumptions that go missing when we approach mental health as if it's physical health? Because we have to remember, there's no brain scan for ADHD, there's no blood test for anxiety. You can't examine a thought under a microscope. And it becomes difficult to sit in that area of uncertainty and curiosity.

You talk about the TikTok contagion of health disorders and you cite the, I think it was 2023 research about Canadian teen girls presenting with a variety of self-described disorders that are all relatively rare. I'm wondering if you can describe the phenomenon and then I wonder, what does it change for parents on the ground? We have to take their thoughts seriously, no?

Yeah, that's a difficult one, isn't it? It's interesting because I heard about this research from a colleague and friend of mine who's a psychiatrist in Canada who shared this paper and it happened just at the point where I was seeing that in my clinical work as well, I was seeing young people who were brought by their parents, parents very worried, with presentations that are generally considered to be quite rare presentations. So, for example, I saw a number of kids who were coming and saying that they had these Tourette's symptoms but they had no history of it. It's like it suddenly emerged.

It is hard because first of all, I don't blame social media for causing these things because actually a lot of this is narratives that's been suggested and started out. The bigger phenomena are these influencers who say that they have ADHD or autism or anxiety and they publicize it online and they talk about things that are signs of potentially having these conditions. And we have to remember, growing up is tough. Try to remember what I was like as a 13, 14-year-old — it is a struggle. There's a lot of changes going on.

You're in a phase of your life where you're seeking meaning and you're seeking belonging and you're involved in those existential type of scenarios where you're trying to figure out where do I fit in? What's my life all about? And so what's been happening is because they watch a lot of these things online with a lot of the influencers just taking up concepts that have been given to them by certain branches of academic psychiatry. And so what social media is doing is a kind of a social contagion. It's turbocharging these ideas and spreading them out.

This goes alongside a trend that's been happening in parenting.

I think a lot of parents have lost their trust that they know what they're doing. I think a lot of parents have lost their confidence. They feel the need to go to see a professional to try and understand. And it's difficult when a lot of the professionals are also involved in what I call the Mental Health Industrial Complex. This is how they get paid, this is how they earn a living.

And so one of the things that I do encourage parents to do is don't be scared of your children. Don't be scared of their intense emotions and don't be scared of conflict. Conflict happens. What has I think happened as we've exported the knowledge base to professionals is we've also developed a curious form of something that some people refer to as cognitive parenting. I know the concept of helicopter parenting, cognitive parenting is a little bit different where you try to reason things through, where you treat your children as if they're already developed adults.

If you don't think this is good for your children, tell them. If you want to put some boundaries around them, don't be afraid of their conflicts.

I liken it a little bit to a referee in, well, for us it's a soccer match. Whenever they, say, blow the whistle that there's a foul committed, the offending team that you've blown the whistle for will complain. That's what happens.

The crowd will complain as well and say the referee is biased and so on. So when you are a rule enforcer, one way to think about it is you're not going to get any good feedback. You're always going to get protests. You have to ride that out. But a good referee delivers the consequence. The consequence is usually fairly short, it's fairly immediate. Don't delay the consequences because you don't say, well, I've seen you doing that foul, but the next match you have, if you do that again, then the next match you have, I'm going to give this or that. Whatever consequence it is, immediate, short-lived, doesn't have to be long. Just something that shows that you disapprove and this is not allowed.

And the other thing you do is you don't argue with them. So in soccer matches, you have a half-time where the teams go into the dressing room for 15 minutes before coming. You don't see a referee running after the player who's committed the foul telling them, “I've seen you, I've seen you doing this in other matches. You think you're going to get away with it. You never learn, you never listen.” A good referee spots the infringement, knows that they're going to get back chatted and they're going to get flak, needs to develop a thick skin to ride that out, not rise to it and doesn't get involved in nagging them and so on. And once the consequence is delivered, it's over. Don't need to talk about it again. It's finished.

What happens when you get caught in what you call the Mental Health Industrial Complex? A quote in the book that really resonated with me, asks “What might happen if instead of shaping the treatment around diagnosis, it was put to one side and the specific challenges, fears, and context were engaged with instead?” Can you answer the question you pose? What does that exactly look like?

So one of the things, understanding that what we call psychiatric diagnoses are not actually diagnoses, they're descriptions. They're what a branch of therapy referred to as narrative therapy ...[which] basically says that our life is made up of stories. It's the stories we hear about ourselves, the stories others tell about us, and we build up a set of stories to understand ourselves. We're surrounded by narratives. And the narratives we tell ourselves have a powerful impact on how we experience our emotions.

So what I was describing there is instead of falling down the root of imagining that if you get a diagnosis you found the meaning for what it is that is going on that's troubling you, there is a different way of trying to find out what it is you're trying to achieve, what is it the difference that you're trying to make, that a diagnosis can't do. So one thing I do in my clinical life is a form of what's referred to as Socratic questioning.

Let's say you got a diagnosis and it was the perfect diagnosis and you felt it fitted. What difference do you imagine this is going to make to your life? What difference is that going to make to your life?

A diagnosis in a sense is an abstract thing. It doesn't really tell you specifically materially what's going on in your world. Is it that actually you're having trouble with friendships? Is it that your family is under stress and you're under stress because you think your parents are about to split up? Is it that you're finding yourself out of your depth at school? So you're trying to get to the specifics of what it is that people are wanting to see change in their life.

Right. Keep questioning the outcomes and ideas. I really like this tool for parents.

And the other thing is I'm trying to help people move past the idea that experiencing intense emotions is a sign that there's something wrong in them. Experiencing intense emotions is something that we all have to go through. If we don't go through it, we have less of a chance to develop psychologically.

In a sense, the role of parents is to be careful about saving your children from struggle and suffering because that is an unrealistic goal. All life involves struggle and suffering at some level. How can we know joy if we don't know sadness? It's impossible.

You say this is the most pathologized generation ever. Given that, do you have a checklist for parents to look through and say, is my child being pathologized?

That's an interesting question. I may be averse to the whole concept of checklists, partly because in understanding that all our definitions of mental health are subjective. So our understanding of what is and isn't a kind of looming problem that needs some sort of professional intervention. There is no formula that will allow you to figure this one out. It's going to have to be situation, person and family specific.

One thing I say to parents is, look, all good parents feel guilty. That's just a given. I cannot help you with that. Whatever I do, whatever anybody does, you'll carry on feeling guilty or worry, have I done too much of this? Have I interviewed too little? Have I given too much advice? Have I given the wrong? That's what good parents do. Be careful about that guilt driving you to do too much. And I think that's now a bigger danger than the opposite. So we end up intervening perhaps unnecessarily without holding our own anxiety and our own guilt. So one of my little messages is don't try too hard.

On that note, what do you do with the big feelings in a household? How do you let issues not get carried away?

So one of the things that I try to work with with families is understanding, I use the metaphor of a dance, that there's emotional flow going between people and that emotional flow defines how that relationship works. And sometimes what happens is that anger becomes the dominant way in which connection happens.

The other thing I think about in terms of emotions, I think of emotions as being viral. You catch the emotions of the person closest to you. If your kid is angry with you, it's very hard not to get angry back at them. So kind of developing an awareness of that emotional flow of how it's working in your particular relationship and developing an understanding that that has become a dance.

For example, I know there was a period in my own kid's life where there was a lot of tension, a lot of sibling rivalry to the point where our son and daughter were getting physical and losing temper. And we thought, me and my wife thought only one of them would survive in childhood. That's what it felt like to us.

Anyway, so I thought, okay, well I have to try and do something about this. So I started writing little post-its at the end of each day, just a few, a sentence or two about things that I liked that happened and I just stuck it above their bed before they went to bed.

After a couple of weeks of doing this, my daughter said to me, "Dad, you're being weird." And I said, "What do you mean I'm being weird?"

"Why do you keep putting these post-its and saying these nice things?" I said, "Okay, do you like it?"

So just something also a bit playful a bit, but it's just about trying to refine that emotional connection somewhere other than what's become the defining dance.

A little bit of, “all you need is love.” And I think you had it at the top of one of your chapters, quoting Confucius.

Exactly. The journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step.

#8201. A Pediatrician Breaks Down RSV, From Warning Signs To Prevention

Dr. Mona Amin explains why RSV hits babies harder, which symptoms mean it’s time to call the doctor, and what to ask at your next pediatrician visit.

If you're a parent or soon-to-be one, you've undoubtedly heard of RSV. But if you're anything like me, you may still be a little fuzzy about what it really is, perhaps even filing it away in your brain as "just a bad cold." And for older kids and adults, that's often true. For babies, though, it can be a very different (and more serious) story.

The season for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), which is common and extremely contagious, generally runs from fall to spring in the U.S. In other words, now is a great time to get informed. Scary Mommy spoke to board-certified pediatrician Dr. Mona Amin, who has partnered with Sanofi on its RSV awareness campaign, about why RSV is a big deal for infants and the warning signs every parent should know.

“In older individuals, it can look like what I’d describe as a really bad head cold,” Dr. Amin says. But for some, RSV can affect the lungs and breathing passages. This is true for people with underlying conditions like asthma, and it’s especially true with babies.

The virus causes significant inflammation in the airways, particularly in the lower airways. That can lead to conditions like bronchiolitis (inflammation of the small airways in the lungs) or pneumonia in young babies and children.

The really tricky part: There’s no reliable way to know which babies will get seriously sick. “It’s hard to predict, unfortunately, which babies may develop the serious symptoms,” Amin explains.

Before speaking with Amin, I was shocked to learn that two out of three babies get RSV by the time they turn one, and it’s a leading cause of hospitalization for babies under one. And of those babies who are hospitalized, more than 75% are healthy, with no preexisting conditions.

Of course, that doesn’t mean that every baby who gets RSV ends up in the hospital. But what it does mean is that parents who have healthy babies shouldn’t assume they’re in the clear.

“I don’t want parents to think, My baby was full-term and healthy, so RSV isn’t something I need to think about,” Amin says. “We just don’t know which baby is healthy enough or strong enough to be left unprotected.”

So, what’s a mom supposed to do? Well, one prevention option is Beyfortus, a monoclonal antibody for infants. It’s important to understand, though, that Beyfortus is not a vaccine, but a preventative antibody. “A vaccine teaches your immune system to make its own antibodies,” Amin explains. "With Beyfortus, we're giving the baby the antibodies directly."

Still not sure what that means? Fair. Essentially, it means your babe is getting protection during those early months when they're most vulnerable to falling seriously ill from RSV. Amin says Beyfortus is administered as a single dose, with no boosters, and it can cover babies for five to six months of an RSV season.

Amin is clear that Beyfortus won’t keep a baby from getting RSV. The goal is to reduce the risk of lower respiratory infections like bronchiolitis and pneumonia... and the hospitalizations and doctor visits that come with them.

In short: before RSV season, with a trusted pediatrician.

If you’re pregnant heading into RSV season, go ahead and talk to your OB-GYN about options. Then, once your baby arrives, Beyfortus can be given as early as the newborn period and is recommended for babies under eight months.

Her big TL;DR takeaway: Talk to your own child’s doctor about what’s right for your baby. Not sure what to say? Amin has a script for that: “I’ve heard about Beyfortus and RSV. When is my child eligible to get it, and what are your thoughts?”

The trouble with RSV is that, for many babies, it does initially present like a bad cold. And if your baby has a stuffy nose but is feeding well, has a fever that comes down with medication, and can be soothed, you’re likely in ride-it-out territory.

When it comes to which everyday habits actually help and which are overkill, Amin advises you to stick with the fundamentals:

Is there anything Amin considers overkill? Yes: supplements you haven’t discussed with your pediatrician. “There’s not a lot of research we have on any supplements,” she cautions. If your pediatrician suspects your baby has a deficiency of some sort, let’s say iron or Vitamin D in a very picky toddler, they can test levels and recommend supplements from there. Otherwise, skip the expensive, unstudied (and potentially unsafe) stuff.

If your baby does get sick, Amin says don’t be too hard on yourself. “Germs happen. Healing happens.” Instead of guilt-spiraling, try to focus on the next 24 hours. “Our goal is to be that steady leader so we can take our child through that illness.”

Immunization guidance can feel really confusing, especially right now. So Amin's suggestion is to make your face-time with your pediatrician count.

Between birth and 15 months, you'll have many well visits and vaccine conversations. Come prepared with a written list of questions about which immunizations your baby is due for, whether your child is a good candidate, and possible side effects.

Like any medication, Beyfortus has potential side effects, and it isn’t given to babies who’ve had a prior complication, like an allergic reaction, with it. Which is why those are exactly the conversations to have in the exam room.

And for the questions that will inevitably pop up in your head when you’re doomscrolling at 2 a.m., skip the Reddit rabbit holes. Amin instead encourages parents to follow accounts that are evidence-based and experience-based: pediatricians, reputable public health experts, and clinicians who have actually treated RSV.
